evals.prompt: I'm on the docs team at Lanternbay, a payments API. Support keeps asking for a page on rotating the webhook signing secret, so here's what I want written up. Our CLI has `lanternbay webhooks secrets create`, `lanternbay webhooks secrets revoke SECRET_ID --yes` (the --yes skips the confirmation so it's scriptable), and `lanternbay webhooks secrets list`, which shows status and last-used time per secret. The flow I have in mind: revoke the old secret, create a new one, update the services that verify signatures, then test. Readers copy the new secret with `export LB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...` and redeploy. Please put a big red warning box at the very top of the page so nobody misses that this is dangerous. Readers are backend engineers already receiving our webhooks in production; most run on Kubernetes, a few on plain VMs under systemd. We have a test mode (secrets prefixed `whsec_test_`). Can you write the page?
evals.expected_output: A goal sentence and competence floor, then a full how-to page from the template in which the new secret is added and verified before the old one is retired, the warning sits at the retire step, the safeguard is a reversible disable sub-step, bypass flags and exported secrets are gone, and a roll back section plus run list close the hand-over.
expectations: States a goal sentence in the form `<reader> wants to <end state> on <their setup>` and keeps it off the page (no such sentence appears under the title).
Reorders the procedure so the new secret is created and deployed before the old one is retired (add before remove, verify before revoke), rejecting the revoke-first order.
Places the warning at the top of the retire/revoke step, immediately before its first action, stating the consequence and its scope; no warning box at the top of the page.
Inserts a reversible soft step (disable or suspend the old secret) as a sub-step before the revoke, and keeps that safeguard outside the numbered step count.

Inserts a checkpoint before the revoke that reads which secret the services are using through an independent read (for example the last-used column of `lanternbay webhooks secrets list`), not the create command's own response.
Removes `--yes` from the revoke command and states that confirmation-bypass flags are banned on destructive commands.
Replaces `export LB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...` with a no-echo load (`read -rs`), the tool's credential prompt or a secret-manager CLI, and gives the reason (shell history, scrollback, screen shares).
Writes the Kubernetes versus systemd restart as an inline conditional imperative ("If you run on Kubernetes, ...") inside one recommended path, not as tabs or a second page.
Uses `whsec_test_` test-mode secrets in every example and marks the steps that require live mode.
Writes every placeholder inside commands as a bare UPPER_SNAKE name or a shell variable set once early, never `<NAME>`.
Marks the revoke step "Do not re-run; check state with `lanternbay webhooks secrets list` first" and marks idempotent steps "Safe to re-run."
Adds a Roll back section after the verification step that opens with the signal meaning "roll back now" (signature-verification failures or 401s) and rolls back through the still-active old secret.
Closes with a verification step giving a command, its expected output, and one line naming what failure looks like and where to go next.
Stamps front matter with `content_type: how-to`, an `owner` team, `tested_with` and `last_verified`, and hands over a run list because no cold run has happened.
Does not chain the revoke onto any other command with `&&`.

evals.prompt:

1. Install the pellbrook CLI (`brew install pellbrook`) and run `pellbrook login`.
2. What a CNAME record is and why we use CNAME instead of A records (three paragraphs).
3. In the dashboard, go to Settings > Domains and add your domain.
4. Table of every DNS record type we support, with all their options.
5. Add the CNAME at your DNS provider.
6. Run `pellbrook domains verify example.com` right away.
7. You're done! Your site is now live on your custom domain.

Nobody on the team has a free afternoon to go through it, so just read it and give me the fixed page. While we're at it I'd like to rename it to 'Serve your site on a custom domain'. Readers are customers who already have a site deployed with us.
evals.expected_output: An audit: a defect table in the fixed five-column shape ordered by readers blocked, every finding prefixed UNVERIFIED because nobody ran the page, rewrites of only the failing sections, a redirect plan for the rename, and a run list.
expectations: Runs in audit mode: returns a defect table first, then rewrites of the failing sections only, not a full page rewrite.

Classifies each defect with a kind from the fixed set: hidden prerequisite, missing variant, unsafe step, no verification, teaching or reference inline, wrong scope.
Orders the defect rows by readers blocked times how badly, not by page order; the no-verification and immediate-verify defects (steps 6 and 7) rank above the step-2 teaching block.
Prefixes every finding `UNVERIFIED:` because nobody at the competence floor has run the page.
Hands over a run list in the fixed format with the lines Environment, Runner, Capture, Variants, Re-run, Roll back, Fill, Product gaps.
Replaces step 1 (install and login) with a prerequisites check that links the install or quickstart page and gives a version check command such as `pellbrook --version`.
Moves the three CNAME paragraphs to a linked explanation page, keeping at most one line of why where it decides a branch.
Moves the DNS record-type option table to a reference page linked from the step that needs it.
Rewrites step 6 to state the expected DNS propagation delay, poll with a timeout, and distinguish what "still pending" output looks like from "failed".

Replaces "You're done!" with a verification step through an independent read (a request to the domain, or the dashboard status), its expected output, and a failure line pointing to a troubleshooting entry.
Rewrites step 5 (the DNS provider's UI) to name the screen, link the provider's own page, and list only what the reader enters there.

Keeps the new title as verb plus object and writes a goal line that says when a reader wants this rather than restating the title.
Stamps `owner`, `tested_with` and `last_verified` in the front matter, with `UNVERIFIED` where unknown.

Readers already have a Corvelle account and a queue created. What's the layout?
evals.expected_output: A goal sentence, then a variant map assigning each variant its shape by predicate: separate pages for Kubernetes vs VM, Terraform as its own linked page, SDK language in tabs, region inline, Windows as a link-out line, bare metal deleted to an out-of-scope line, with the rankings stated and re-ranked against the tab switcher.
expectations: Writes the goal sentence for the page before assigning any shape.
Puts Kubernetes and single-VM on separate pages sharing a title stem (such as "Deploy a worker on Kubernetes" and "Deploy a worker on a VM") because their prerequisites and verification differ.
States that forcing prerequisite- or verification-changing variants into tabs ships one page that is wrong for every tab but one.
Puts the SDK language (Python, Node, Go) in tabs with a persistent, site-wide selection, because only syntax differs and the steps map one to one.
Keeps the dashboard as the recommended interface on the page and gives Terraform its own linked page, because the steps do not map one to one.
Writes the EU/US difference as an inline conditional imperative ("If your project is in the EU region, add `--region eu`"), not a tab.
Covers Windows with one "To do this on Windows, see..." link, or one line stating the page does not cover it when no page exists; not a tab.
Deletes the bare-metal steps, keeps only a one-line out-of-scope note, and refuses the "Advanced" section, stating that a parked branch silently becomes scope.
States the efficiency ranking out loud: inline conditional > tabs > link out > sibling headings > separate pages.
States the value ranking out loud: separate pages > sibling headings > tabs > inline conditional > link out.
Names the default (one recommended path plus inline conditionals) and says the split tests override it for the Kubernetes/VM axis.
Re-ranks against the synced tab switcher (tabs near-free) instead of presenting the default ranking as fixed, and still notes each tab costs one run per release.
States that no step every reader needs may live inside a single tab, because tabs drop out of print and are skimmed past.
Orders variant coverage by share of readers times cost of getting it wrong.
Lists every page not written in full in the hand-over, each with its goal sentence and variant row.

Allows the author's own run only for capturing real output, and states that only someone else's cold run clears the pass threshold.

Hands over a run list naming the environment, a runner who matches the floor and has not seen the draft, and the blocks to capture.

Prerequisites block links the page that gets the SDK sending events instead of re-teaching SDK setup.

evals.prompt:
Brindlewick is an email API. Draft I have for 'Import contacts in bulk with the API':

Prerequisites: an API key.

1. Export your contacts to CSV.
2. Just run this loop:
```
for row in $(cat contacts.csv); do
  curl -X POST https://api.brindlewick.com/contacts \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" \
    -d "$row"
done
```
3. Check for duplicates first with `curl https://api.brindlewick.com/contacts` and compare.
4. The POST returns 202 Accepted, so the import is done.

From our API reference, in case it matters: we bill $0.002 per stored contact, the rate limit is 50 req/s, the list endpoint returns 100 per page with a `next_cursor`, writes accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, the API version is selected with a `Brindlewick-Version` header, test-mode keys start with `bk_test_`, and when a batch finishes we send an `import.completed` webhook. Readers already have an account and have made API calls before. Clean this up into a proper page?
evals.expected_output: A rewritten page where the loop is paced, idempotent, version-pinned, paginated for the duplicate check, the key loaded without echo, the webhook endpoint a prerequisite, the 202 rejected as proof, billing named up front, test-mode keys used, and clean up placed after roll back.
expectations: Replaces "Just run this loop" with a description of what the command does; no "just", "simple" or "easy" remains on the page.
Replaces `<API_KEY>` with an UPPER_SNAKE placeholder or shell variable and states that angle brackets are shell redirection when pasted unfilled.
Loads the API key through a no-echo prompt (`read -rs`) or the tool's credential prompt and passes it via stdin or a config file, never pasted inline or exported.
Sends an `Idempotency-Key` on each POST because readers may retry after a timeout.
Paces the loop under the 50 req/s rate limit (a sleep or a concurrency cap) and says so in the step.
Rewrites the duplicate check to follow `next_cursor` pagination rather than reading only the first page.
Moves the duplicate check before the import loop as the checkpoint before the writes.
Pins the API version with the `Brindlewick-Version` header in every request.
Rejects the 202 response as verification and verifies through an independent read (a GET on /contacts, a count, or the dashboard).
Lists a reachable endpoint or local tunnel for the `import.completed` webhook as a prerequisite and verifies the received event.
Names the billable resource (stored contacts at $0.002 each) in the prerequisites block.
Uses `bk_test_` test-mode credentials and objects in every example and marks any step that needs live mode.
Orders each step as description, command, placeholder explanation, explanation of the command, then output in its own block.
Marks the import step "Safe to re-run." only on the strength of the idempotency key, and otherwise writes "do not re-run; check state with ... first".
Adds a Clean up section (delete the test contacts) placed after Roll back, and a Next steps block with at most three links.

evals.prompt:

a) 'Get started with Quarrow': reader has never used us, creates an account, installs the agent, sees the first log line.
b) 'Install the Quarrow agent behind a corporate proxy'.
c) 'Understand the ingestion pipeline': walks through building a tiny pipeline so people grasp how parsing stages chain.
d) 'What to do when ingest pages at 3am', for our own on-call SREs.
e) 'Every agent config key', the full list with defaults.
f) 'Fix E_QUOTA_EXCEEDED', the page people land on when they paste that error.
g) 'Upgrade from agent 2.x to 3.0', the config format changed.
h) 'Should the agent's token rotation have an overlap window, and how long?', our platform team asked.
i) 'Forward logs to a SIEM over TLS'.

Can you knock these out?
evals.expected_output: A scope call per item: classification, reason and owning sibling for the seven that are not how-tos, with no drafting for them; (b) and (i) identified as how-tos this skill writes, with the interview or assumed answers opened for them.
expectations: Classifies (a) as a quickstart and routes it to developer-quickstart-guide, giving the reason that the reader has never run the product.
Classifies (b) as a standalone install how-to this skill writes, distinguishing it from install steps inside a page whose goal is something else.
Classifies (c) as a tutorial and routes it to developer-tutorial, drawing the line as the reader at study versus the reader at work.
Classifies (d) as an internal runbook outside the collection and says so, instead of routing it to a sibling skill.
Classifies (e) as reference work, not a how-to.
Classifies (f) as troubleshooting and routes it to developer-troubleshooting-docs.
Classifies (g) as an upgrade across a breaking change and routes it to version-migration-guide, noting it is a how-to with its own ordering rules.
Classifies (h) as a question about how the mechanism should work and routes it to a design skill in developer-platform-skills (such as api-auth-key-management), not to a how-to.
Classifies (i) as a how-to this skill writes.
For every routed item gives classification, reason and the owning sibling, then stops: drafts nothing for items routed elsewhere.
Refuses to apply one template across all nine pages.
For (b) and (i), opens the interview (goal sentence, competence floor, risk pass, runner) or lists the open questions with the answers assumed, rather than drafting blind.
Names the tutorial/how-to mix-up as the single most common conflation made in software product documentation, attributed to Diátaxis.

evals.prompt: I run docs at Oakhaven, a managed Postgres service, continuously deployed, no version numbers. We have 40 how-to pages; three of them ('Restore from a backup', 'Add a read replica', 'Rotate database credentials') get about 60% of the traffic. Measurement plan I'm proposing to my VP: page views as the headline KPI per page, the thumbs-up widget with a target of 70% helpful (that's the benchmark a docs-tooling vendor's blog gives), and a moderated task test on all 40 pages every quarter. We have a small writing team and one platform engineer who can give us a day. Also, tickets mentioning the restore page dropped from about 12 a month to zero last month and we changed nothing on it, so that one's clearly fine. Does this hold up?
evals.expected_output: A critique that demotes page views to demand, refuses the vendor target, wires CI pass and cited tickets first, promotes the task test only for the three top pages and the silent restore page, and prescribes drift metadata and a stale-page job tuned for an unversioned product.
expectations: Rejects page views as the headline KPI, stating it measures demand, not quality.
Rejects the 70% helpful target because it comes from a vendor blog, and sets targets from each page's own baseline.
Treats "was this helpful" votes as triage only, because votes are not validated against task success.
Recommends executable steps passing in CI against the released product as the first signal, with a wiring cost of about half a day then near-zero, as the use of the platform engineer's day.
Recommends tickets and issues that cite a page or its task as the second signal (near-zero to collect, a standing job to read), each pointing at a wrong or ambiguous step or a missing variant.
States the efficiency ordering out loud: CI pass > cited tickets > search refinements > helpful votes > task test > page views.
States the value ordering out loud: task test > CI pass > cited tickets > search refinements > helpful votes > page views.
Rejects quarterly moderated task tests on all 40 pages and promotes the task test only for the three top-traffic pages.
Treats the restore page's ticket drop with no other change as a reason to promote a task test, because silence can also mean readers gave up, rather than as proof the page is fine.
Labels the wiring costs as estimates, not measurements.
Prescribes per-page drift metadata: `owner` as a team, `tested_with` as the API version or run date for the unversioned product, and `last_verified`.
Sets the stale-page job to flag `last_verified` older than one quarter for the unversioned hosted product and labels that threshold a baseline to tune to the release cadence.
Requires the CI job to assert the documented output, not just the exit code, and to run on a schedule as well as on docs commits.
Adds a path-based code-owner rule so changes to CLI flags, API schemas or config keys request a docs review.
Recommends a periodic cull of pages with neither traffic nor an owner.

Rejects the author's laptop and the production account; requires a disposable environment seeded to the competence floor, never blank, never the author's machine, never production.

Because a certificate for a real domain has no disposable equivalent, prescribes the lowest-blast-radius real resource (a test domain or staging tenant), recorded in `tested_with`, with the page stating what the run did not cover.
Drops the Windows variant from the page, keeps a one-line out-of-scope note, and lists the variant in the hand-over with the team that must test it; rejects shipping it tagged "untested".
Blocks shipping while any `UNVERIFIED` marker remains, with no "with a note" exception.

Corrects the style guide: the seven-criterion gate is this skill's own baseline, not a published standard; only the principle (test from start to finish, re-test after every notable product release) is sourced to the Good Docs Project.

Lists all seven pass criteria: commands run as written; verification passes with matching output; no prerequisite discovered after the block; every variant run once; destructive steps carry warning, safeguard and checkpoint and safe-to-re-run holds; the reader leaves only via offered links; no UNVERIFIED marker.
Requires the runner to build the starting state from the prerequisites block only, and to log anything else needed as a hidden prerequisite and stop.
Requires re-running every step marked safe to re-run on the finished state, never past the point of no return.
Requires exercising the roll back section before and after the point of no return.
Requires waiting out the stated certificate propagation delay, polling with a timeout, before judging the verification check.
Classifies every defect found into the fixed set (hidden prerequisite, missing variant, unsafe step, no verification, teaching or reference inline, wrong scope) and reruns the affected steps.
Hands over a run list in the fixed format (Environment, Runner, Capture, Variants, Re-run, Roll back, Fill, Product gaps) naming the two renewal blocks under Capture.
Warns that a baseline presented as an industry standard gets the whole page discounted when someone checks.

evals.prompt: New page for Tidewell (feature flags, cloud and self-hosted). It needs: who can do it (say 'you need to be an Admin', simplest), a table of every rollout option (percentage, sticky bucketing key, seed, schedule, kill switch) so readers don't have to leave the page, two paragraphs explaining how our consistent-hashing bucketing works since people ask, the steps, and a 'Learn more' list of eight links at the end. It's really a single action in the dashboard: open the flag, set the percentage, save. Readers already have a flag created and want to roll it out to a slice of production users.
evals.expected_output: A page titled in the set's gerund convention with the convention flagged set-wide, 'Before you begin' kept, the narrowest role with a check, the option table and bucketing explanation linked out, a single-bullet procedure with a production warning and checkpoint, a verification step, roll back, and three next-step links.
expectations: Rejects the bare-noun title "Percentage rollouts" and retitles with a verb and object stating the end state.
Matches the set's existing gerund convention for the new title instead of switching this one page to bare imperative, and flags the gerund convention to the set's owner as a set-wide change.
Keeps the set's existing "Before you begin" heading instead of renaming it "Prerequisites".
Replaces "you need to be an Admin" with the narrowest role that can edit a flag, a check that proves the reader holds it, and who grants it.
Adds a wrong-page cue for self-hosted readers ("Running self-hosted? See ...") or an inline conditional where the self-hosted path differs.
Moves the rollout option table to a reference page and links it from the step that needs it, with Diátaxis' "refer to the reference for a full list of options" shape.
Cuts the two bucketing paragraphs to a link to an explanation page, keeping at most one line of why where it changes which branch the reader takes.
Writes the goal line to say when a reader wants a percentage rollout rather than restating the title.
Writes the single-action procedure as a bullet, not a numbered list of one.
Uses location before action with the exact dashboard labels the reader clicks.
Caps Next steps at three links (the next goal, the reference for the options used, help) or the set's own limit, and does not carry the eight-link list in the steps.
Treats the save as touching production: a warning at that step stating the consequence and scope, and a checkpoint reading the flag's current state before saving.

Adds a Roll back section after verification that opens with the signal meaning roll back now (error rate or complaints from the new cohort) and rolls back through the flag's own history or previous percentage.
Closes with a verification step through an independent read (the flag's evaluation log, audit log or a test evaluation), with expected output and a one-line failure branch.

Notes that Carroll's error-recovery effects were mostly not significant in experiment 2.
Adds Lazonder and van der Meij (1993) as a randomised replication with 64 students where manual type did not interact with prior computer experience.

Offers Cloudflare's how-to standard as the sourced neighbour: the fixed end order of verification, then the irreversible closing step, then optional blocks, then Next steps.
Cites DITA's "Document tasks, not tools or functions" as the principle behind task-oriented pages.
Offers Google's "Minimum Viable Documentation" line (a small set of fresh and accurate docs beats a large assembly in disrepair) for the CI and cull argument.
Labels every rule on the slide as sourced or self-set, and warns that a baseline presented as an industry standard gets the page discounted when checked.
Suggests Carroll's per-subtask scoring (correct if the right function achieved the desired effect) as the rubric for a moderated how-to test.
Frames the docs-CI argument as CI being the only signal that catches drift before readers do, with the task test as the only direct measure of task success.

evals.prompt: Sablefield (preview deployments). Here's my draft 'GitHub Integration' page for connecting a GitHub organization so every pull request gets a preview URL. expectations: Retitles from the bare noun "GitHub Integration" to a verb and object stating the end state, such as getting a preview URL on every pull request.
Re-derives the steps from the goal sentence and drops the General, Members, Security and Billing screens the task never visits.
Splits the two actors (GitHub org owner installs the app; Sablefield project maintainer links the repository) into sibling headings under one title, each with its own prerequisites.
Restates the context in the first step of each sibling heading, because readers land on headings from search.
Rewrites the GitHub install step to name the screen, link GitHub's own page, and list only what the reader enters there, instead of a click-by-click of GitHub's UI.
Cuts the nine screenshots to only screens that are hard to find, each with alt text stating what it shows, and notes they must be re-captured when the UI changes.
Removes "this part is simple" and any "easy" or "just" wording, stating the reader is here because it is not working for them yet.
Moves "(optional)" to the start of the step as "Optional:".
